name: Brain Abscess

likely: Staphylococcus aureus (especially post-neurosurgery or hematogenous spread)
Enterobacteriaceae (especially with otogenic or sinus source)
possible: Nocardia, Toxoplasma, or fungal causes in immunocompromised patients (broader workup needed)
pathogens.why: Brain abscess pathogens reflect the presumed source: contiguous spread from sinusitis/otitis/dental infection brings streptococci and anaerobes, hematogenous spread (e.g., from endocarditis) brings S. aureus, and post-neurosurgical abscesses carry a different staphylococcal/gram-negative profile. Immunocompromised hosts require broader consideration including Toxoplasma and fungal causes.

investigations.why: Confirms the diagnosis, localizes the abscess, and is essential for surgical planning; MRI is more sensitive, particularly for early/cerebritis-stage lesions.

investigations.test: Stereotactic aspiration or surgical drainage with culture
investigations.why: Provides definitive microbiological diagnosis and is often therapeutic, particularly for abscesses >2.5cm.
May identify the organism in hematogenous spread, supporting de-escalation.
Screens for infective endocarditis as the source, which would change the overall management plan significantly.

investigations.test: HIV testing (if risk factors or atypical presentation)
investigations.why: Relevant given the broader differential (e.g., toxoplasmosis) in immunocompromised hosts.

reason: Headache with focal neurological deficit or seizure and fever, without prominent meningismus, raises strong suspicion for brain abscess. This requires urgent neuroimaging (contrast CT or MRI) and empiric antibiotic therapy covering the likely polymicrobial source, alongside urgent neurosurgical consultation for possible drainage - antibiotics alone are often insufficient for abscesses requiring surgical source control.

clinicalPearls: The classic triad of headache, fever, and a focal neurologic deficit is present in fewer than half of cases, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1178).
Headache is the single most common symptom (more than 75% of patients), typically a constant, dull ache that becomes progressively more severe and refractory to treatment (p.1178).
Fever is present in only about half of patients at diagnosis; its absence should not be used to rule out a brain abscess (p.1178).

Most patients present a relatively long time after symptom onset (commonly around 11-12 days), and a brain abscess usually behaves like an expanding mass lesion rather than an obvious infection (p.1178).
Meningismus is generally absent unless the abscess has ruptured into the ventricle or infection has reached the subarachnoid space (p.1178).
Diffusion-weighted MRI helps distinguish abscess from tumor: an abscess shows restricted diffusion (high DWI signal, low ADC) within the cavity, whereas necrotic tumors typically do not (p.1178).
Lesion location predicts the source and the deficit: otogenic abscesses favor the temporal lobe and cerebellum, while sinus and dental abscesses favor the frontal lobes (p.1179).
New-onset partial seizures are the most common manifestation of neurocysticercosis, an important focal CNS lesion in patients from Latin America (p.1181).
harrison.pathophysiology: Intact brain parenchyma is relatively resistant to infection; bacterial invasion generally requires preexisting or concomitant ischemia, necrosis, or hypoxemia in brain tissue. Abscesses arise by direct contiguous spread (sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis, dental infection), by inoculation after penetrating trauma or neurosurgery, or by hematogenous seeding from a distant focus; about a quarter are cryptogenic with no identified source. Hematogenous abscesses are often multiple, frequently lie at the gray-white junction in the middle cerebral artery territory, and tend to be poorly encapsulated. Once established, the lesion evolves through stages: early cerebritis (days 1-3, perivascular inflammation around a core of coagulative necrosis with marked edema), late cerebritis (days 4-9, expanding necrotic center with macrophage/fibroblast infiltrate and a developing thin capsule), early capsule formation (days 10-13, capsule better formed on the cortical than ventricular side, correlating with the ring-enhancing appearance on imaging), and late capsule formation (day 14 onward, dense collagenous capsule, regressing edema, and surrounding gliosis with reactive astrocytes that may underlie later seizures). In right-to-left cardiac or pulmonary shunts, bacteria bypass the pulmonary capillary filter while shunt-related hypoxemia and polycythemia create ischemic nidi favoring abscess formation (p.1178-1179).
additionalDifferentials: Primary or metastatic brain tumor (the major consideration when fever is absent)
Cerebral infarction or hematoma (can resemble abscess on CT/MRI)
Tuberculoma (a major cause of focal CNS mass lesions in India and East Asia)
infectionMimics: Cerebral toxoplasmosis (reactivation, mainly in immunocompromised/HIV hosts)
Nocardial, Aspergillus, Candida, or Cryptococcus CNS lesions in immunocompromised hosts
additionalInvestigations: MRI is preferred over CT, being superior for detecting early (cerebritis-stage) lesions and posterior fossa abscesses (p.1178).
Diffusion-weighted imaging with apparent diffusion coefficient mapping to separate abscess (restricted diffusion) from tumor (p.1178).
Gram stain plus aerobic, anaerobic, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures of abscess material obtained by CT-guided stereotactic needle aspiration (p.1179).
Inflammatory markers: peripheral leukocytosis in about half, elevated ESR in about 60%, and elevated C-reactive protein in about 80% of patients (p.1179).
Serum IgG antibody to Toxoplasma gondii when imaging suggests toxoplasmosis (p.1181).
Enzyme-linked immunotransfer blot as a confirmatory test for neurocysticercosis, plus funduscopic examination in suspected cases (p.1181).
redFlags: Lumbar puncture should NOT be performed when a focal intracranial infection such as abscess or empyema is known or suspected, because CSF analysis adds nothing and LP increases the risk of herniation (p.1179).
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilledema, nausea/vomiting, drowsiness or confusion) can dominate the presentation, particularly with cerebellar abscesses (p.1178).
Rupture of an abscess into the ventricle (heralded by new meningismus) is an ominous development (p.1178).
High risk (about 35%) of focal or generalized seizures (p.1180).
Glucocorticoids and prior treatment can alter the CT/MRI appearance of the capsule, potentially masking or modifying the imaging picture (p.1178).
harrison.prognosis: With modern neuroimaging, stereotactic aspiration, and improved antibiotics, mortality has fallen to typically less than 15% in recent series. However, significant sequelae - including seizures, persisting weakness, aphasia, or mental impairment - occur in at least 20% of survivors (p.1180).
pitfalls: Relying on the classic triad: headache, fever, and focal deficit coexist in fewer than half of patients (p.1178).
Excluding the diagnosis because the patient is afebrile - fever is absent in roughly half of cases (p.1178).
Performing a lumbar puncture in a patient with a suspected focal intracranial infection, risking herniation without diagnostic benefit (p.1179).
Misreading a ring-enhancing lesion as tumor when diffusion-weighted imaging would point to abscess (p.1178).
Forgetting that glucocorticoid therapy can alter the imaging appearance of the abscess capsule (p.1178).
Overlooking cerebral toxoplasmosis, which characteristically reactivates and causes ring-enhancing lesions in HIV-infected and other immunocompromised patients (p.1181).
Dismissing a cryptogenic abscess as having no source - many are in fact attributable to occult dental infection (p.1179).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison describes a staged histopathologic/radiologic evolution rather than a clinical severity score: early cerebritis (days 1-3), late cerebritis (days 4-9), early capsule formation (days 10-13, when ring enhancement appears), and late capsule formation (day 14 and beyond) (p.1178).
